newsitem.title: UK: EURO PRODUCTS OUTLOOK - CRUDE FALL TO PRESSURE.
newsitem.headline: EURO PRODUCTS OUTLOOK - CRUDE FALL TO PRESSURE.

text.p: Most European oil products look set to come under some pressure this week if crude continues to fall but for gasoline, which is expected to stay stable.
Prompt gasoline may remain buoyant, despite Morgan Stanley's widely perceived lifting of its squeeze on Friday.

"The market will probably stabilize next week," an oil major said. "We've seen an awful lot of downward movement over the last one or two days, but there is no reason to expect this slide to continue."
Prompt Eurograde values gained $25 between Friday August 1 and last Wednesday before retreating by $18-$20 since.
The major agreed with the view that the physical market remained tight as refiners struggled to meet end-user demand in a still active driving season.
Others said that demand which was held back during first half August would begin to support prompt quotes as the second half approaches.
Dealers said naphtha would continue to weaken on the back of an expected easing of crude, pointing to little end-user demand in the north and a closed Med arb to Asia.
The outlook for gas oil is uncertain and dealers said liquidity was likely to be poor.
Poor seasonal demand could be revived if IPE gas oil futures continue to weaken.
Heating oil barges were likely to trade flat against September IPE or up to $1.00 against August while diesel looks set to hover around $5.00 above the screen.
Expectations of Russian material arriving in Rotterdam should keep a lid on barge.
High sulphur fuel barges are expected to come under some pressure due to the end of loading delays at two storage faciliaties and incoming Russian material from the cargo market, traders said.
"I see the market declining rather than rising," one trader said. "Some Russian M-100 cargoes will be discharged in the barge market."

But a few traders were more optimistic, saying that prompt material remained in short supply and that would give support. High sulphur barges last week reached the $96 to $97 mark, levels unseen since March.
High sulphur cracked cargo levels, which rose to trade at $85 fob last week, will follow crude.
"If crude continues weakening then some pressure should set in," a trader said.
Low sulphur fuel cargoes, which remain in short supply, will be steady with sellers sticking to the swaps level of $96/$97.
